votes.why: the shoreline animals look like repeated, simply modeled 3D assets.
the smooth, uniformly shaded foreground boulders and the tiny repeated deer models look like a typical CG landscape render, not a photo.
the stiff duplicated 3D-model animals along the shoreline with unconvincing water contact
the foreground boulders repeat the same distinctive angular shape and diagonal cracks.

The rocks are too smooth and the water reflections look procedural. The tiny deer are copy-pasted, so this reads as a polished but individual-artist CG landscape rather than a film-grade frame (b is the close second).
the conspicuously regular concentric ripples where the animals meet the water.
smooth uniform CG pebbles and stylized extinct camelid creatures look like a polished standalone 3D paleo render rather than film footage or a photo
the smooth, procedurally textured foreground pebbles lacking natural micro-detail despite the clean path-traced lighting
the upright animal’s head is a blunt wedge with no visible eyes, ears, or mouth.
the polished lighting, water reflections and ripples look like high-end CG, though the repetitive pebbles and slightly stiff animal models leave (c) as a close second.
the two drinking animals look like scaled copies of the same posed 3D model.
the animals look smooth and plasticky, like CG models, against a photoreal landscape, which reads as a well-made but ordinary 3D render (paleoart-style scene) rather than a photo or a film frame.
the stiff 3D-modeled creatures standing in the water without ripples or displacement
the two drinking animals have almost exactly the same silhouette, as if one posed model was scaled and reused.
The water and rock lighting is very detailed and filmic, but the stiff, slightly waxy animals look CG, which points to a high-end render (film or cinematic) and away from a photo.
the foreground’s uniformly sharp, repeating rock texture.
the skeleton and the shore texture look like a CG render (tiled, smeared surface detail and a dinosaur skeleton placed on top), clearly not a real photo but short of film-level detail.

the foreground skeleton and sharp procedural waterline lack the micro-detail and ground integration of a real photo or top-budget film while showing the polished lighting and textures of a standard 3D render
the same cluster of dark cave openings repeats across the distant cliff like a tiled texture.

The atmospheric lighting and grading are good, but the ground is a repetitive procedural fiber texture and the water edge is smeared. The skeleton is also crudely modeled, so it reads as a competent but ordinary CG render, not a film-grade or photographic image.
the water’s uniformly smeared reflections look like a generic render shader.
the creature necks have smooth, plain skin with simple shading, which looks like a decent but ordinary 3D render and not film-grade work, even with the realistic cliffs and water.
the smooth procedural water bulge and spikes intersecting the surface without foam or realistic fluid interaction alongside blurry low-detail foreground creature textures.
the water around the surfacing creature forms a smooth rubbery bulge rather than breaking into ripples.

the believable water reflections, volumetric haze and warm cliff lighting look like high-end cinematic CG, though the simple creature skin and slightly soft rock detail leave some chance it's an ordinary 3D render (c).
